catalog_quote: [Eades 1976:25, carried by StressTyp2 passage 878] Most words have initial main stress. Some words have primary stress on the second syllable; most of these words have a long vowel in the second syllable. There is no secondary stress.. Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word. Words that are still used in communities are often pronounced with stress on a long vowel on the final syllable.. In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated.. It is possible that …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the Besold 2012:113-114 passage is verbatim in the held ch.3 text at the stated section; the Eades 1976:25 passage is present only as StressTyp2-carried text (we hold no Eades file; IA copy is lending-restricted, search-inside still returns 'Item not available' today, Google Books shows no pages). (2) Deciding source: a 2012 ANU dissertation (philological language-recovery grammar) plus a 1976 salvage grammar sketch; for a language with no fluent speakers since mid-20th c. these are the best that can exist, and Glottolog's 5 descriptive refs contain nothing better (Mathews 1902/1903 are the raw stress-marked wordlists Besold already analyses). It mentions Dhurga only as the language of Brown's, Cipollone's and Lane's programs on the NSW south coast. No phonology, prosody, accent or stress content of any kind; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the chapter.
